items.note: Fragmentary Prakrit kāvyas praising Bhoja as hero, donor and liberal are found inscribed on stones at Dhār and Ujjain.
items.gloss: Other Prakrit poems (Kurmashataka II, Kodandakavya, three Khadgashatakas, many fragmentary ones) also call Bhoja brave, generous and liberal; these are graceful and clear; these poem fragments are found on stone slabs at Dhar and some at Ujjain.

items.note: Bhoja's fame as ideal: Kumārapāla of Gujarat liked to be called 'laghu Bhojarāja'.
items.gloss: Bhoja was an ideal in virtues for friends and foes alike; they too felt pride in being likened to Bhoja; King Kumarapala of Gujarat liked to be called 'little Bhojaraja'.

reject_reason: comparison of a Kashmir king with Bhoja in Rajatarangini verses; only a passing reference to Malwa's lord, no usable span

items.note: Poets praised patrons as 'Nava-Bhoja-rāja'; a later (late-13th-century) descendant was praised as 'Bhoja like another Bhoja' - memory of Bhoja as model.
items.gloss: Hence poets praised their patron with the epithet 'New Bhojaraja'; a descendant of this Bhoja, another king Bhoja at the end of the thirteenth century, was praised by comparison with this ancestor: 'Bhoja is Bhoja's equal'.

items.note: Bhoja as hero of popular tales and puppet-tales; 'Bhoja-vidyā' came to mean jugglery; much remains to be collected and studied.
items.gloss: His skill in thought-transference and jugglery became so widespread that 'Bhoja-vidya' came to mean indrajala; like Vikramaditya he became hero of popular tales, songs and legends, with miraculous stories woven round him, e.g. in Rajavallabha's Bhojacharitra (15th century) where he turns from man into parrot; collecting and studying these tales is still needed.

items.note: Prabandhacintāmaṇi's 104 buildings/works/titles of Bhoja, supported by a fragmentary 1258 CE inscription of Jayavarmadeva naming 104 Meru/Trikūṭa-type prāsādas; discussed in Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra chs 55-56.
items.gloss: According to Prabandhachintamani Bhoja's 104 buildings, works and titles had the same name; this is confirmed by a fragmentary inscription of Jayavarmadeva (1258 CE) saying Raja Bhoja built 104 prasadas such as Meru and Trikuta; the rest is broken; it confirms Prabandhachintamani to that extent; these prasadas are discussed in Samarangana-sutradhara chapters 55-56.

items.note: Later authors cite Bhoja as author on Ayurveda, astronomy, grammar, lexicon, poetics and drama.
items.gloss: Bhavaprakasha and Ruchiviniscaya call him an Ayurveda author; Keshavarka an astronomy author; Kshirasvamin, Sayana and Mahipa a grammarian and lexicographer; poets praise his poetic ability; Shabdasamrajya is composed on Bhoja's grammar; Karyayem in the Shakuntala commentary calls Bhoja a knower of drama like Bharata.

items.note: Mallinātha quotes Bhoja's works; Prabhāvakacarita lists Bhoja's subjects, taught in schools.
items.gloss: Commentator Mallinatha cites Bhoja's works on political science, grammar, lexicon, poetics, astrology and conduct; Ramachandra Budhendra calls him like Dhanapala a master of all literature; Prabhavakacharita gives a list of Bhoja's works on many subjects, which were then taught in schools.

items.note: Tradition that Bhoja composed quickly; Prabandhacintāmaṇi and a 17th-century verse (Rāmacarita in one night).
items.gloss: Bhoja could compose works on diverse subjects very quickly; Prabandhachintamani underlines this; a 17th-century writer, Chudamani Dikshita, says Bhoja composed the Ramacharita in a single night, which Chudamani completes with the Yuddhakanda in one day.

items.note: Argument that composing many works was not impossible for Bhoja; descendant Arjunavarman and others confirm his talent.
items.gloss: Jayasimha Siddharaja's court poet also says he composed a mahakavya in one day; skilled composers could write a whole poem in a day; Raja Bhoja was such a composer, so composing works on various subjects together was not impossible for him; others including his descendant Arjunavarman confirm Bhojadeva's talent.

items.note: Dhārā had 84 prāsādas/crossroads (Prabhācandra); 1258 CE Jayavarmadeva inscription: 104 prāsādas of Meru, Trikūṭa etc.; number 104 attested by literature and inscription.
items.gloss: According to Prabhachandra Dhara had 84 palaces and as many crossroads; per Jayavarmadeva's inscription of 1258 CE Bhoja had 104 prasadas such as Meru and Trikuta; so the number 104 is confirmed by both literature and inscription.

items.note: Bhoja's imperial titles and epithets in copper plates, inscriptions and colophons (Mālavacakravartin, Dhāreśvara, Tribhuvananārāyaṇa etc.); twelve subordinate kings.
items.gloss: Bhoja was Maharajadhiraja Parameshvara, for his works show twelve kings under him; the title appears in his copper plates, inscriptions and colophons; he bore epithets such as Malavamandana, Malavadhisha, Malavachakravartin, Sarvabhauma, Avantinayaka, Dhareshvara, Tribhuvananarayana, Ranarangamalla, Loknarayana, Vidarbharaja, Ahiraja, Abhinavarjuna, Krishna.

reject_reason: list of Bhoja's work titles and epithet-names with truncated 1258 Modi inscription reference; no usable claim

items.note: Start of the list of works attributed to Bhoja: Campū-Rāmāyaṇa, Śṛṅgāramañjarīkathā, Avanikūrmaśataka, Vāgdevīstuti etc.
items.gloss: List of works known under Bhoja's name: 1. Literature: (1) Champu-Ramayana, (2) Shringaramanjarikatha, (3) Avanikurmashataka, (4) Subhashitaprabandha, (5) Vagdevistuti, (6) Vidyavinoda, (7) Shalikatha, (8) Mahakalivijaya.

reject_reason: bare continuation of a list of titles (philosophy, astrology, dharmashastra) with no explanatory content

items.note: Architecture (sthāpatya) works attributed to Bhoja: Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra or Vāstuśāstra, and Yuktikalpataru.
items.gloss: 12. Architecture: (1) Samarangana-sutradhara or Vastushastra, (2) Yuktikalpataru.

items.note: Prakrit poems attributed to Bhoja are all fragmentary, inscribed on stone and found at Dhār.
items.gloss: 14. Prakrit poetry: (1) Kodandasanghata, (2) Avanikurmashataka, (3) Khadgashataka (three), (4) an unnamed poem (all fragmentary, inscribed on stone and found at Dhar).

items.note: The devices described in the Dhārā passage of the Śṛṅgāramañjarīkathā are given a technical treatment in the Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra, with some going beyond it.
items.gloss: The marvellous devices and arts scattered through the description of Dhara in those tales receive their technical exposition in the Samarangana-sutradhara in almost the same wording; the tale presents some devices not specified in the Samarangana-sutradhara, a further elaboration.

items.note: Bhoja worshipped Vāgdevī in his works and had her image made in 1034 CE.
items.gloss: Bhoja not only wrote a whole poem in praise of Vagdevi; she is also saluted in Sarasvatikanthabharana, Shringaramanjari and other works; in 1034 CE Bhoja had a charming image of Vagdevi made.

items.note: Later authors cited Bhoja's works across poetics, dharmaśāstra, astrology, medicine, Śaiva philosophy, grammar, music and drama.
items.gloss: Later authors kept quoting Bhoja's works as authority, whether poetics, dharmashastra, astrology, medicine, Shaiva philosophy, grammar, lexicon, polity, music or drama; clearly Indian scholars have continually given Bhoja special regard.

items.note: Commentaries on Bhoja's Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa and Tattvaprakāśa; Bhoja himself commented on the Yogasūtra, Amara and Manu.
items.gloss: The Sarasvatikanthabharana on poetics became popular as an alamkara text and many commentaries were written, some published; also on the grammar and on the Shaiva-philosophy Tattvaprakasha; Bhoja himself wrote commentaries, e.g. on the Yogasutra, Amara and Manu.

items.note: Bhoja's Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa śālā at Dhārā as a centre of learning, with a similar one at Ujjain.
items.gloss: Raja Bhoja built at Dhara a hall called Sarasvatikanthabharana, in the tradition of Vatsyayana's Kamasutra directive, a world-famous centre of education, literature and learning; a similar centre existed at Ujjain.

items.note: Many Prakrit poems of Bhoja are inscribed in stone.
items.gloss: Several Prakrit poems composed by Bhoja, lord of Dhara, are inscribed on stone; their language is simple and graceful.

items.note: Subhāṣitaprabandha of 255 Sanskrit verses: first subhāṣita anthology.
items.gloss: Bhoja's compiled Subhashitaprabandha is the first subhashita collection of 255 Sanskrit verses on varied subjects; the rest came later; though short it has historical importance, since it began the Sanskrit subhashita-collection stream.

items.note: Bhoja's lexicon Nāmamālikā is published, revealing little-known word meanings.
items.gloss: A dictionary composed by Bhoja called Nammalika is published; it reveals several little-known word meanings.

items.note: Bhoja's Tattvaprakāśa regarded as an authoritative Śaiva-philosophy text, published with commentary.
items.gloss: Raja Bhoja's Tattvaprakasha is regarded as an authoritative text of Shaiva philosophy; it is published with commentary.

reject_reason: publication notes on Bhoja's philosophical and astrological works and verses on lamp-offering; no bearing on any unit

items.note: Bhoja's astrological work Rājamṛgāṅka composed in Śaka 964 (1042 CE).
items.gloss: Bhoja's astrological work Rajamriganka, published in Brahmavidya (4/3), was composed in Shaka 964 (1042 CE).
